title: Text to numbers
summary: Tokens and the embedding table: how text becomes vectors.

steps.text: A GPT never sees letters. The tokenizer turns the text into ids, one per position. This model's {{V}}-token vocabulary makes most words a single token, usually including the space before it (`␣upon`). The chips under the prompt are the positions: this model reads up to **100** of them.
steps.prompt: Once upon a time, there was a little girl.

steps.text: Each id picks one row of the **token embedding table** `wte`: a lookup, not a calculation. The heatmap shows the rows picked for this prompt, one per position. Rows are positions, labelled with their token; columns are the {{d}} dimensions of the vector.

ask.question: Click any cell in the row for **␣upon** (position 1).
ask.hint: Rows are positions, counting from 0: Once, ␣upon.
ask.correct: The breakdown under the heatmap shows the value is copied straight from the `␣upon` row of `wte`.

steps.text: The same token always gets the same row. This prompt has **␣a** twice (“upon a time”, “was a little”): both rows are identical, because the lookup knows nothing about where a token sits.

ask.question: Click a cell in the row for the second **␣a** (position 7).
ask.correct: Compare its colours with row 2: the same vector.

steps.text: The whole table lives in the network atlas: top-left, `token table wte`, one row for each of the {{V}} tokens in the vocabulary. Everything the model knows about a token before reading its context is in that row.

Zoom in on the top of `token table wte` in the atlas (outlined in gold): a band of vertical stripes. Those rows belong to tokens that **never occur** in the training text, mostly single bytes such as `�`, `=` and `@`. They started out random, but now they are almost the same vector, so each column is one colour.

ask.question: Why would tokens the model never saw end up identical?
ask.hint: This model ties its embeddings: `wte` is also its output layer.
ask.correct: Every training step pushes down the score of every token that is not the right answer. A token that never appears is never the answer and never an input, so that push is the only thing that ever changes its row, and it is the same push for all of them. They all converged on one direction, away from anything the model predicts.
